title: OK: Lowering the Bar Even Further For Teaching
author: Peter Greene
summary: Greene looks at Oklahoma's new law letting districts keep adjunct teachers, who need only a high school diploma, in classrooms without the earlier hour limits. He sets it against the state's long record of losing teachers through low pay, low spending and public disrespect. Reactions from a college of education dean and State Superintendent Joy Hofmeister show that the promised highly-trained professionals have not appeared and that the degree requirement was dropped with little awareness. Greene argues the policy fits a privatizing, anti-union, low-spend agenda in which degrading public school teaching makes charters and vouchers look better. He grants that alternate pathways can be valuable but says this goes far beyond that, and that a 2017 survey of lapsed certificate holders shows respect and autonomy, not red tape, are what keep people out.
points: Oklahoma answered a retention crisis by redefining who counts as a teacher instead of fixing pay, respect or working conditions.
The adjunct rule leaves district leaders to define distinguished qualifications, and the dean of education reports he is not seeing them.
Greene reads the move as McDonaldization: a larger pool of replaceable, cheaper staff weakens unions and makes private alternatives look better by comparison.
A survey of Oklahomans with unused teaching certificates found two thirds would need respect, autonomy and professional treatment, not just more pay, to return.
quotes: Oklahoma has had trouble holding onto teachers for quite some time. A 2018 report found that over the previous six years, 30,000 Oklahoma teachers had left the classroom. Keep in mind that the state only employs about 52,000 teachers. Oklahoma has real trouble recruiting and retaining.

Oklahoma had a category called "adjunct teacher," a designation awarded to someone who had nothing but a high school diploma. But an adjunct teacher had limitations, allowing only 270 clock hours of classroom teaching per semester. Last January, Senator Jessica Garvin (former nursing home administrator) decided to fix that by proposing that the limitation be axed, and school districts allowed to stick adjuncts in a classroom for as long as they liked.

Seriously, lawmakers? Exactly which highly-trained professionals did you imagine were going to jump at the chance to make less than $50K for doing teaching, which is--and I can't say this often enough--a really, really hard job to do when you're an amateur.

Hofmeister said when someone enters school having previously owned a Hallmark store, they don’t have the experience and training to step into a second-grade class. “There are some who really seem to think that what is happening in school is a lot of babysitting,” Hofmeister said, “and it’s not. Kids don’t get back these days. They need to be spent with those who have the expertise to deliver an excellent education, and we have to do more.
Alternate pathways to the class are not automatically a bad thing, and being able to tap professional expertise can be a big benefit for schools. But this measure goes far beyond that.

Oklahoma (and other parts of the country) didn't dig this hole overnight, and they won't fill it overnight, either. But solutions like "just let anyone fill the job" is just digging the hole deeper and deeper.
